$comment: The bill of materials, as data. /hardware/ renders this; check-links.mjs verifies every url and writes back the `checked` block. Prices are approximate single-unit hobbyist figures and are NOT verified — only the links are. Edit here, never in the HTML. `usd` is the named part linked here; `usdGeneric` is the same chip on an unbranded module. `tools` is the bench, ordered by priority for someone starting with only a soldering iron.

checked.how: tape/check-links.mjs — GET each url, follow redirects, match `expect` against the page title

verdicts.ok: 200, and the page identified itself as the right part
verdicts.resolves: 200, but the title is JS-rendered or bot-walled so identity could not be machine-checked
verdicts.blocked: the vendor refuses automated requests (403/503). Works in a browser; open it yourself

parts.name: ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1
parts.spec: ESP32-S3-WROOM-1, 8 MB flash, 8 MB PSRAM (N8R8). N16R8 also fine — the audio lives on the SD card, so flash size is not the constraint.

sources.note: the official page, for finding a local distributor
the 16 MB variant; Mouser renders in JS so identity is unverified

parts.name: PN532 NFC/RFID breakout v1.6
parts.spec: 13.56 MHz, I²C. Reads and writes NDEF on NTAG213. Ships with a tuned stripline antenna, which is the part that decides read range.
parts.note: Adafruit's is the expensive one. Generic red 'PN532 V3' modules are $6 and use the same chip; the antenna tuning is where they differ, and this project spends its read range on a four-year-old's aim.

parts.name: MAX98357A I²S class-D amp
parts.spec: DAC and 3.2 W mono amp in one part, straight off the S3's I²S. 2.4 mA quiescent.

parts.name: Speaker, 40 mm, 4Ω 5 W
parts.spec: Full-range. Speech in a bedroom; a bigger driver buys bass nobody needs and a bigger box.

parts.name: microSD breakout, 3 V only
parts.spec: SPI or SDIO. The 3 V-only version is right here — the S3 is a 3.3 V part and the level-shifted board just adds parts.

sources.note: the level-shifted one, if you want 5 V tolerance

parts.name: microSD card, 32 GB
parts.spec: Any class-10 card. ~1,200 hours at MP3 64 kbps mono.

parts.name: MCP73871 USB / DC / solar Li-ion charger
parts.spec: True power path: runs the box and charges the cell at the same time. JST connectors for cell and load.

parts.name: Li-ion pack, 2500 mAh, 3.7 V, protected, JST
parts.spec: A packaged pack rather than a loose 18650 — no holder, no exposed cell, and it plugs straight into the charger.
parts.note: A protected 18650 in a holder is cheaper per mAh and replaceable, but it needs a screwed compartment and a JST pigtail you make yourself.

parts.name: 5 V buck-boost (VERTER, TPS63060)
parts.spec: Holds 5 V across the whole discharge curve, so the volume does not sag as the cell empties.
parts.note: See the power chain below — this is choice A, and it is the reason the budget assumes an 18% conversion loss rather than 5%.

parts.name: Panel-mount 10 kΩ linear potentiometer
parts.spec: The safety part. A physical end stop, trimmed once at build time, that a child cannot get past.

parts.name: Arcade button, 30 mm
parts.spec: Back and next. Big enough to hit without looking, which is the whole specification.

sources.note: the LED version, if you want the back button lit

parts.name: NTAG213 stickers, 25 mm round
parts.spec: 144 bytes. A tape card uses 96 of them.

sources.note: 1000-count reel; they sell smaller counts too
100-pack; Amazon does not answer automated identity checks

parts.name: A deck of playing cards
parts.spec: 63×88 mm, paper or PVC. NOT foil or metallic-backed — a metal layer detunes the antenna and the card will not read at all. Test one before you sticker fifty.

parts.name: Perfboard, hookup wire, LED + resistor, SPDT switch, screws

tools.name: Solder, 60/40 rosin core, 0.3–0.8 mm
tools.why: You said you have an iron. Solder is sold separately, and leaded 60/40 is markedly easier to learn on than lead-free — flows at a lower temperature and wets properly. Wash your hands.

tools.name: Digital multimeter
tools.why: The most important thing you do not have. Two of the assembly gates cannot be passed without one — measuring read range is a ruler, but 'is the current near the budget' and 'is this joint actually connected' are not. Continuity beep alone will save this build twice.

tools.name: Wire strippers, 20–30 AWG
tools.why: The biggest quality-of-life jump after the iron. Stripping with side cutters nicks strands, and nicked strands break later — inside a finished box, months in.

tools.name: Flush diagonal cutters
tools.why: For trimming header pins flat against a board. Ordinary side cutters leave a spike that shorts to whatever sits above it.

tools.name: Helping hands with magnifier
tools.why: Soldering a header to a board needs three hands: board, iron, solder. This is the difference between an enjoyable evening and a burnt finger.

tools.name: Perma-Proto half-size board
tools.why: Perfboard laid out like a breadboard, with the same power rails. You can prototype on a breadboard and then solder the identical layout, which removes a whole class of transcription mistake.

tools.name: 0.1" female headers, 36-pin strips
tools.why: THE thing that removes most of the wiring. Every module in the parts list comes with 0.1" pins; solder sockets to the board and they plug in. Four of the fiddliest interconnects stop being cables at all, and a dead module becomes a swap rather than a desolder.

tools.name: JST-XH 2.54 mm kit, pre-crimped
tools.why: Latching, polarised connectors with NO crimper: the pins arrive already crimped onto wire and you push them into the housing. Solder the bare end to the board. This is the whole answer for build one.

tools.name: JST-PH 2-pin cable, 100 mm
tools.why: Battery side. The cell and the charger already terminate in JST-PH, so the highest-current connection in the box needs no work from you at all — but a spare pigtail is worth a dollar.

tools.name: Crimper — NOT YET
tools.why: Buy this for project two or three, when you are making custom lengths often enough to resent the pre-crimped kit. When you do: skip the SN-28B, which is the tool everyone recommends and whose anvil is too wide — it bites into the insulation instead of wrapping it. IWISS IWS-2820M or SN-025 instead. A marginal crimp fails INTERMITTENTLY, months later, and you will blame the firmware.
